topStories.headline: New State Rule Opens CalFresh Food Benefits to Nearly Every SFSU Undergraduate
topStories.dek: A California rule change that took effect in June quietly removed the main barrier keeping eligible college students off the food-assistance rolls — and SFSU's Basic Needs Center has already helped more than 400 students apply this fall.
topStories.body:
San Francisco State University announced on November 2 that most of its undergraduates are now eligible for CalFresh, California's food-assistance program, following a state rule change that went into effect June 1. Under the new policy, any undergraduate enrolled at least half-time in a degree program at a UC, CSU, or California Community College automatically meets the initial eligibility requirements — removing the complicated work-requirement exemptions that had kept many qualifying students from even attempting to apply.

The change is significant for the Lakeshore campus, where housing costs and food insecurity have long pressed students. SFSU's Basic Needs Center said its CalFresh Help Clinic has already guided more than 400 students living on campus through applications this fall semester, allowing many to reduce their campus meal-plan charges in exchange for monthly grocery benefits. A single-person household can receive up to $306 a month.

A separate rule that took effect March 1 also removed financial aid — grants, scholarships, loans, and fellowships — from the income calculation used to determine CalFresh eligibility. That change means students whose only income is educational funding may now show $0 in countable income, further widening the pool of those who qualify.

SFSU's Basic Needs Center operates a CalFresh Help Clinic and can connect students with the application process. Students can also start at BenefitsCal.com or visit the SF Human Services Agency, which lists SFSU as one of three San Francisco campuses with on-site CalFresh support resources.

topStories.headline: CSU Faculty Strike Vote Enters Final Week — Fact-Finding Hearings Run Through Today at SFSU
topStories.dek: The California Faculty Association's strike authorization ballot closes November 19, and the fact-finding hearings that could shape any deal are scheduled this week — including sessions that fell on November 12 and 13.
topStories.body:
The California Faculty Association's systemwide strike authorization vote, which opened October 26, is in its final week with members at all 23 CSU campuses — including San Francisco State — casting ballots through November 19. A majority 'yes' vote would give the union's board authority to call a work stoppage, though passage does not automatically trigger a strike; contract talks can continue.

Fact-finding hearings before a three-member panel were scheduled for November 2, 5, 6, 12, and 13, meaning sessions fell this week at SFSU and elsewhere in the system. The hearings follow 16 months of stalled negotiations and the union's declaration of impasse in July. The main disputes involve faculty salaries, workload, and — a new front in this round — the right of faculty to govern how artificial intelligence is deployed on campus and in classrooms.

The union represents about 29,000 professors, lecturers, librarians, counselors, and coaches across the CSU. At SFSU specifically, the chapter has been vocal throughout the fall. SFSU students have indicated support for faculty: the student union told campus newspaper the Golden Gate Xpress that it intends to back faculty in the event of a strike, as it did during a 2023 walkout.

If the vote passes and CSU management does not improve its offer, a strike could come as early as December. The CSU's last tentative agreement was widely unpopular at SFSU — a World Socialist Web Site report cited a campus poll showing 70 percent of respondents planned to vote against that deal.

topStories.headline: SFSU to Reopen Mary Ward Hall at Half Capacity This Spring, Easing a 99% Housing Crunch
topStories.dek: Housing and dining officials confirmed the spring 2027 reopening of a shuttered residence hall — but the long-term fate of the building, including possible demolition, remains unresolved.
topStories.body:
San Francisco State University's Housing, Dining and Conference Services announced at an October meeting that Mary Ward Hall, one of two traditional red-brick residence halls on campus that had been shuttered, will reopen at half capacity beginning spring 2027. The news was first reported by the Golden Gate Xpress on November 4.

The decision was driven by an acute shortage of on-campus beds. Associate Vice President Jeny Patiño told the student newspaper that SFSU's six housing communities are currently at 99.3 percent occupancy, leaving virtually no room for students who want affordable on-campus housing. Opening Mary Ward at reduced capacity is intended to provide a lower-cost option for first-year students.

The building is currently undergoing cosmetic refurbishments and preventative maintenance ahead of the spring opening. While it has been used for summer sessions, it has been officially closed for the regular academic year. Mary Ward Hall has capacity for approximately 500 students.

Longer-term questions about the hall's future remain open. Patiño noted that the possibility of demolishing both Mary's buildings — Mary Ward and its sister hall, Mary Park — is still under discussion as officials assess aging infrastructure and financing gaps. No decision has been made on that front.

moreNews.headline: Empire Theater Site on West Portal Avenue Set to Become 172-Unit Tower
moreNews.body: The former CineArts Empire Theater at 85 West Portal Avenue is headed for redevelopment as a 12-story, 172-unit apartment building — nearly triple the 64-unit, 9-story proposal that first surfaced earlier this year. Developer DM Development and Empire West Portal LLC revised the project upward in late August to take advantage of state housing-law provisions that limit local design review. The revised plan includes 26 affordable units, 7,000 square feet of ground-floor retail, and rooftop amenity spaces. The SF Standard reported in early September that local merchants — including the owner of BookShop West Portal and the manager of Eezy Breezy grocery — have mostly shifted from opposing the project outright to figuring out how to survive two-plus years of construction on the neighborhood's main commercial strip. The project still requires city approvals.

moreNews.headline: Parkmerced Development Land Acquired by New York Investor After Foreclosure
moreNews.body: Four development land parcels at Parkmerced — San Francisco's largest apartment complex — were acquired this summer by New York-based Yellowstone Real Estate Investments after the previous owner, Maximus Real Estate Partners, defaulted on a $1.8 billion loan. The SF Chronicle reported the sale on July 22. Yellowstone, which had provided a $101 million construction loan for the stalled redevelopment project, took over the parcels, which carry approvals for nearly 1,700 new apartments and include 52 existing units. It remains unclear whether Yellowstone intends to move forward with construction; the rest of the Parkmerced complex continues to be managed by receiver Douglas Wilson Companies and Ballast.
